name: Northeast Buttress

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the glacier and climb steep heather and alder onto the toe of the buttress, pulling on tree roots and turf where the rock disappears.
Gain the toe of the buttress and climb onto the lower rock on a broken but solid rib.
Simul-climb broken slabs and heather benches along the crest; protection is marginal and spaced roughly every 200 feet.
Sustained climbing up the buttress crest and corners on improving, more continuous rock.
Climb a knobby left-facing corner on sounder granite above the crest, requiring careful placements in shallow cracks.
A steeper crux section on the best rock of the lower buttress, the technical high point of the route.
Above the crux, follow a broken rib of solid rock past a large detached block as the buttress begins to lay back.
Mixed rock and snow as the route weaves past hanging glacier terrain, requiring careful route-finding around seracs.
Traverse broken rock and snow benches to the bivy ledges near 7,100 feet at the base of the upper snow arete.
Continue up the long upper buttress on varied ground above the bivy ledges.
Climb the exposed snow arete above the bivy, which drops off steeply on both sides onto the upper glacier; belay off pickets or buried axes.
Finish the technical climbing on a single steep snow or ice headwall pitch, reported up to 200 feet in early-season conditions, before easier snow leads to the summit ridge.

rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the upper East Ridge as it steepens toward a buttress.
hazards: The alternative to the whole rappel sequence is downclimbing the loose gully immediately to climber's right of the rap line - parties on the two lines put rock down on each other, so agree on one or the other before splitting up
rappel_detail.station: At the east end of the summit ridge, after the long loose traverse along ledges below the crest. The first rappel is a full rope-stretcher on a single 60 m down to a big block; parties who want shorter, more controllable pitches split it into two.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the buttress-like section of ridge; loose rock is a constant hazard here.
rappel_detail.anchor: natural (horn/block, inspect any tat before trusting it)
hazards: Several of the wrapped blocks on this ridge are genuinely suspect. Push and check each one is seated before you weight the sling, rather than trusting that it held for the last party
rappel_detail.station: The big block itself - the landing for the rope-stretcher, or the intermediate station if you split it. Most of the anchors from here down are slings wrapped around large blocks.

rappel_detail.notes: Mid-sequence rappel bypassing steep/loose ground beside the ridge crest.
hazards: Old cord and webbing of very mixed age; carry plenty of spare cord and rebuild the worst stations rather than adding to them
rappel_detail.station: First of two or three further rappels working down the crest below the big block.

rappel_detail.notes: Alternative parties instead downclimb a loose gully just to climber's right of this rap line.
hazards: Sustained loose rock - this ridge is a serious descent in its own right, not a walk-off, and most parties take three to five hours on it
rappel_detail.station: Continues down the crest; a 60 m single rope covers every station on this section.

rappel_detail.notes: Progressively nearing the C-J col; ropes should be handled carefully in the loose gully terrain to avoid dislodging rock.
hazards: Wet heather over rock is slick and hides the edges of steps
rappel_detail.station: The last of the crest rappels, ending where the ground turns to heather.

rappel_detail.notes: Second-to-last rappel of the ridge descent, still on loose, exposed terrain.
hazards: A hidden station means the common error here is going too far and having to reclimb loose ground to reach it
rappel_detail.station: After the heather you downclimb rather than rappel, and the next station is slightly hidden - it is easy to walk past it and end up downclimbing ground you should have rappelled. Find it before you commit to descending further.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel reaching the Cascade-Johannesburg col, after which the route joins Doug's Direct traverse back toward Cascade Pass.
hazards: The col and the terrain below it are exposed to anything the ridge sheds - do not regroup directly beneath the rappel line
rappel_detail.station: From that hidden station, the last rappels drop to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, where the route joins Doug's Direct back toward Cascade Pass.

rappels: About 7 rappels on a single 60 m rope down the East Ridge to the Cascade-Johannesburg col (6 to 8 depending on how much you downclimb), then descend via Doug's Direct or Cache Col
descent_text: Descend via the long East Ridge, not a walk-off — it is a sustained, loose, exposed ridge traverse in its own right. From the summit, work east along the ridge, connecting loose 3rd/4th-class ledges roughly 75 ft below the actual crest to bypass a series of gendarmes. As the ridge steepens into more of a buttress dropping toward the C-J col (the saddle between Johannesburg and Cascade Peak), you have two options: rappel a series of anchors along the crest, or downclimb a loose gully just to climber's right of the rap line. Most parties rappel this section — parties describe on the order of 6–8 raps to reach the col (one recent party made two full 60m raps in a gully with natural rock anchors partway and atop the gully; another describes roughly 7 shorter raps off slings/tat on the crest), so bring a 60m rope and a small rack of slings/cord for building or backing up anchors — these are natural anchors (horns, blocks, sometimes fixed webbing) rather than bolted stations, and existing tat should be inspected before trusting it. From the C-J col, the standard descent (locally called "Doug's Direct") traverses beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehills across steep meadows, climbs to the north ridge of Mixup Peak, drops via 3rd/4th-class slabs and blocks to the Cache Glacier, then follows a climber's trail along Mixup Arm back down toward the Cascade Pass Trail and the road — roughly 5 hours from the col to the car. Watch for loose rock throughout the ridge and gully sections, and for the same cold Cascade River ford on the final approach back to the trailhead.
approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road. Rather than taking the maintained Cascade Pass Trail, leave the trail near the parking lot/hairpin area and descend a dirt/brush embankment down to the Cascade River, then ford it — this is a cold, glacial-melt crossing that runs highest in the afternoon on hot days, so an early start (or crossing on the return before flows peak) is worth planning for. From the river, climb up and over the debris/terminal moraine below the peak's northeast face and pick up a boot path. At roughly 3,500 ft you'll reach an obvious snow finger/couloir; follow it up and climber's-right onto the toe of the Northeast Buttress (Rib). Above the snow finger there is no trail — the route is sustained, steep vegetable-and-rock climbing: hand-over-hand up alder in a mossy streambed, steep turf and heather, and short stretches of tunneling through subalpine trees, trending right to gain the buttress/rib crest around 5,000–5,500 ft. From the crest, steep heather slopes lead into 4th-class rock, and the crest is followed (with a few pitches of low 5th class in spots) up to a snow arête that runs nearly to the summit snowfield; parties often bivy around 7,100 ft. In under a mile of horizontal distance you gain roughly 3,500–4,600 ft, so this is one of the steeper, more sustained approaches in the Cascades — expect route-finding through the brush/heather bands, loose rock and moraine underfoot low down, and real rockfall exposure in the snow-finger/couloir section if other parties are above. Water is available at the river ford and from seasonal seeps/snow lower on the buttress, but there is none once you're up on rock.
overview: Johannesburg Mountain's Northeast Buttress is one of the great long alpine routes of the North Cascades: a sustained, roughly twenty-pitch line up the same immense northeast face that drops nearly 5,000 ft in under a mile above the Cascade Pass road. It's rated no harder than 5.8 technically, but carries an outsized reputation among North Cascades climbers — less for pure difficulty than for its relentless length and complex, mixed terrain, including stretches of steep heather and brush low on the route that regulars describe as 'vertical bushwhacking' or 'tree climbing.' Most parties bivy partway up, commonly around 7,100 ft below the final headwall, and the route has a long history of climbers returning a day or two later than planned.
beta: Modern parties climbing the fuller/harder version of the same buttress rate it Grade V, 5.8, AI2: a short approach leads to loose lower slabs, then thousands of feet of near-vertical vegetation (alder, turf, heather), a 5.5-5.8 rock band to a ~7,100 ft bivy, an exposed snow arête, and a short ice pitch to the summit ridge.
gear: single to double rack of cams to 3 inches
fa: 1957, by the Western Rib start (party not recorded). The left-hand 1951 rib is a separate route.
